papers.summary: Large reasoning models (LRMs) achieve strong performance by externalizing explicit reasoning traces before producing the answer, yet suffer from overthinking challenge that allocates uniformly heavy computation to queries of varying difficulty. While proprietary models mitigate this via opaque routing, open-source LRMs still lack an efficient mechanism to internalize adaptive reasoning due to both expensive training cost and limited disclosure of training recipes. In response, we introduce RPO (Root-token Policy Optimization), a framework that enables LRMs to self-determine when to reason by training only the initial root token (e.g., whether to invoke the <think> tag) via group relative reward and group-wise advantages. By focusing on this pivotal branching point, RPO drastically reduces training overhead and VRAM usage. Across multiple model families and scales, RPO learns difficulty-aware adaptive thinking at just ~2% of the training compute of prior adaptive-reasoning methods.

papers.title: Memory Echo in Single-Agent Long-Term Memory: Lifecycle Evaluation and Provenance-Guided Mitigation
papers.authors_text: Yufeng Li, Sheng Yao, Peng Zeng, Dezhang Kong, Shi Lin, Changting Lin, Xun Wang, Meng Han
papers.summary: Long-term memory supports agents across sessions. Repeated retrieval and write-back can let one historical claim occupy multiple retrieval positions and influence current answers without independent evidence. Existing work examines retrieval, updating, and question answering, leaving same-source record accumulation and post-correction persistence underexplored. Motivated by research in social cognition and memory psychology on repeated exposure, retrieval, and revision, we define \emph{Memory Echo} as the excess retrieval exposure gained by historical information from the same source without additional independent evidence, and introduce MEchoBench to evaluate its emergence, correction resistance, persistence, and effect on answers. To address this phenomenon, we introduce the Family--Provenance--Authority framework (FPA). Specifically, FPA selects one representative per source family, conditions the eligibility of old records for the answer context on verified corrections, and constrains final answers with authoritative evidence. In paired replay on 190 fixed questions across four memory frameworks, FPA raises accuracy from 0.825 to 0.920 with DeepSeek V4 Flash and from 0.782 to 0.916 with Kimi K2.6; mean Decision Contamination Effect falls from 0.106 to 0.030 and from 0.109 to 0.038, respectively. These results show that agent memory can preserve traceable history without allowing repeated historical information to govern current decisions. The code is available at https://github.com/OrcasSam/memory-echo-benchmark.

papers.title: Autonomous 3D Visual-Thermal Inspection for Utility-Scale Solar Farms
papers.authors_text: Lachlan Tychsen-Smith, Mark Cox, Brett Wood, David Haddon, Kenrick Anderson, Benjamin Duck, Jim O'Malley, Noel W Duffy, Peyman Moghadam
papers.summary: Utility-scale photovoltaic (PV) inspection is dominated by aerial surveys, which are effective for identifying module-level hot cells but provide limited visibility of critical components located under the array, including connectors, cabling, fasteners and structural elements. These assets are difficult to inspect consistently at scale, and their defects are often spatially small, partially occluded and difficult to localise from isolated images. We present an automated 3D visual-thermal inspection system (Tricorder) for under-panel PV asset inspection. The approach combines LiDAR-inertial Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) with geometrically calibrated RGB and thermal imagery and machine-learning-based object detection and segmentation. Detected assets are associated with the reconstructed 3D environment, allowing visual and thermal observations from multiple viewpoints to be spatially fused and localised. We demonstrate the approach on utility-scale PV data for MC4 connector detection and connection-state recognition, thermal anomaly identification, and detection of structural components including bolts, nuts and torque tubes. The results demonstrate a pathway from image-based inspection toward spatially grounded autonomous inspection, where defects are detected and linked to specific assets and their 3D locations within the solar farm.

papers.title: Gaussian Process Bandits for AI System Optimization with Selectively Verified Feedback
papers.authors_text: Shuang Wu
papers.summary: Gaussian process bandits exploit similarities among configurations to optimize prompts, retrieval systems, and agent workflows. In these applications, however, inexpensive model-based evaluations can disagree with trusted task outcomes. We study selective verification when an action is chosen before a diagnostic is observed and trusted feedback is informative on an unknown set of diagnostic states. A finite reliability class and a finite RKHS signal dictionary describe these two sources of uncertainty. We construct a fixed audit design that combines reliability coverage with reward separation and establish a finite-time regret bound that accounts for a hard audit budget and the rounds needed to obtain informative observations. A safe adaptive extension mixes this robust design with predictable Chernoff allocations while preserving a uniform identification floor and exact expected acquisition-cost accounting. For signed-coordinate kernels, structured and diffuse reliability classes require different audit scales despite sharing the same reward geometry. Synthetic experiments distinguish these certified designs from an adaptive posterior heuristic and GP controls. Safe adaptive allocation reduces aggregate regret relative to the fixed design under the exact dictionary, but its finite-budget error certificate is numerically loose. Conditional-feedback errors can remove the heuristic's advantage and target perturbations can reverse it. Separate AI-task replays assess feedback correction and fitted-dictionary policies without establishing end-to-end validation of a learned selective-verification method.

papers.title: Instructions Are Evidence, Not Objectives: Measuring Outcome Alignment of Agents
papers.authors_text: Kaiming Liu, Yuxuan Liu, Jinrui Ju, Minyuan Ruan, Xuanyu Lei, Peng Li, Yang Liu
papers.summary: Large language model agents can follow complex human instructions to solve real-world tasks. In practice, however, initial instructions are often incomplete. In our analysis of 100 user-agent trajectories from SWE-chat, 56\% of initial instructions omit requirements that later emerge as necessary, and 52\% of the useful follow-up requirements could have been inferred from the project. A user states requirements from their own understanding of the task, and these \textbf{stated requirements} often differ from the \textbf{true requirements} that completing the task imposes. An agent should therefore treat the instruction as evidence rather than as the objective, inferring the true requirements from the instruction and the environment and satisfying them even when the user is not yet aware of all of them. We call this ability \textbf{outcome alignment}. In this work, we construct \textbf{TiGanEval}, a benchmark of software engineering and research tasks. In every task the user genuinely lacks part of the requirements, each requirement stays discoverable from the code and runtime behaviour of the environment, and requirements the agent infers are separated from those the user adds after observing delivered work. These properties together make outcome alignment measurable. Evaluating eight frontier models including GPT-5.6-Sol, we find outcome alignment broadly missing: the models lose 53 to 67 points of success rate when moving from the full specification to the partial instruction, and consequence feedback across four submissions does not close the gap. Furthermore, a plan-mode harness cannot compensate for the missing ability of the model itself, which places outcome alignment among the abilities the next generation of models should be developed for.

papers.title: Degrees of Freedom in Multi-Agent Coordination: Between Centralized and Decentralized Regimes
papers.authors_text: Yiqing Peng, Hehai Lin, Zixuan Wang, Dongyi Zhang, Zhengjie Zhu, Yi Han, Yangyang Zheng, Hao Wang, Qian Li, Chengwei Qin
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) are commonly organized around two coordination regimes. Centralized coordination provides explicit control but can create a bottleneck at a single coordination locus, whereas decentralized coordination offers local autonomy but must achieve effective collaboration through distributed decisions and experience. These trade-offs motivate a systematic study of the space between the two regimes. We introduce Degrees of Freedom (DoF), a continuous configuration framework that quantifies the size of the decision space delegated to downstream agents. DoF controls the granularity of delegated work and the target probability that each task unit is assigned to the branches. Its endpoints recover the two coordination regimes. Across multiple task domains, DoF reveals a hierarchy of organizational effects. Delegated granularity and within-regime routing produce structured but bounded profile reallocations, whereas task domain and retained experience are associated with stronger differences between the centralized- and decentralized-branch profiles. The resulting performance landscape is task-dependent: different domains favor different DoF configurations, while atomic-target conditions are more consistent across runs. In-domain retained experience brings the two branch profiles closer together. The same controlled sweep reveals a task-dependent coordination landscape: some domains exhibit higher-performing configurations, whereas others show flatter responses and no single configuration dominates across domains. In five of the six evaluated state, an intermediate DoF configuration achieves higher mean accuracy than both endpoints, demonstrating the value of exploring the coordination space between them. Together, these findings provide empirical guidance for studying and designing intermediate coordination regimes in LLM-based MAS.

papers.title: Learning Robot Policies for Whole-Body Mobility Assistance via Dynamic Human Motion Generation
papers.authors_text: Shikun Ban, Shohei Nagai, Qingyang Song, Hanxi Wan, Eric Zhao, Thomas Wang, Zackory Erickson
papers.summary: Robotic assistance for human mobility could benefit care recipients and reduce caregiver burden during physically demanding tasks such as Sit-to-Stand (STS) and Lift-and-Transfer (L&T). Learning robot policies for these whole-body assistive tasks is challenging: real-world data collection for human-robot interaction is costly and safety-critical, making simulation an attractive alternative. Prior work, however, typically treats the human as static or minimally responsive and thus fails to capture the cooperative nature of mobility assistance. We present a simulation-based framework for learning whole-body assistive robot policies. At its core is a human policy trained with an adversarial motion prior that produces realistic care-recipient motion in response to the robot's actions. A human-adaptive scripted controller interacts with this policy to collect diverse robot demonstrations at scale. From these demonstrations, we train 3D diffusion policies that map segmented human point clouds and robot joint positions to whole-body actions for a mobile manipulator, without relying on privileged human state at deployment. The resulting robot policies successfully perform both STS and L&T assistance in simulation. Preliminary experiments further demonstrate sim-to-real transfer for STS after fine-tuning on a small amount of real-world data. Videos are available on our project page: https://rchi-lab.github.io/human-gen-mobility-assistance/

papers.title: I3L: Iterative Interactive Imitation Learning for Whole-Body Mobile Manipulation
papers.authors_text: Wensi Ai, Christopher Luey, Karthik Dharmarajan, Evans Han, Yunfan Jiang, Stef Ren, Jianwen Xie, Jiajun Wu, Li Fei-Fei, Ruohan Zhang
papers.summary: Policies trained offline from teleoperated demonstrations can degrade outside their training distribution. This gap is particularly acute in long-horizon whole-body mobile manipulation, where long horizons amplify compounding errors and coordinated arm, torso, and base motion makes exhaustive demonstration coverage impractical. We introduce I3L, an integrated hardware and learning system that combines whole-body correction with iterative policy refinement to address this last-mile reliability gap. Its low-cost, open-source JoyLo+ interface uses policy-tracking leader arms and touch-triggered takeover to enable coordinated corrections across the body parts, while iterative deployment and retraining allow operators to target failures of the updated policy. We evaluate I3L across three robot embodiments and eight simulated and real-world tasks, including four long-horizon whole-body mobile manipulation tasks. Controlled simulation experiments show that four-round HG-DAgger achieves the highest final success on both tasks. Under this protocol, I3L improves autonomous success over the base policies by an average of 68.3 percentage points and achieves at least 90% success on every task, outperforming demonstration-only training by 35.6 percentage points on average with the same number of training trajectories. Averaged across tasks, takeover duration per episode decreases by 72% over four rounds. Together, these results show that I3L helps close the last-mile gap between offline training and reliable deployment and provides practical insights into collecting and using corrections for long-horizon whole-body mobile manipulation. Videos, visualizations, and appendix are at https://i-3l.github.io/.

papers.title: Auditing Failure Attribution: Label Predictability and Judge Behavior
papers.authors_text: Tianyang Xu, Jing Gao
papers.summary: Failure-attribution benchmarks ask an LLM judge which step or agent caused a failure. A high score should mean the judge checked the faulty step against the run (a cross-step check). However, spurious signals (surface cues) that predict the annotation can produce a high score. In this paper, we propose four tests to separate checking from cue use. Input restriction asks whether partial input predicts the annotation. Cue following checks whether moved cues change answers. Residual accuracy scores judges where cue-only predictors fail. Aggregation asks whether the failure mix or metric changes rankings. Real observations motivate these tests: on three benchmarks, simple predictors match or beat GPT-4.1. In two Who&When Pro systems, a classifier reading one step's reasoning finds 95-100% of faulty steps, motivating input restriction. In one of them, error injection leaves no reasoning after the faulty step; judges fine-tuned on its labels beat GPT-4.1 by 41 points. Adding task-related reasoning after that step moves this cue: fine-tuned judges lose 31-99 points, but zero-shot judges lose at most 9, motivating cue following. On Aegis, blaming every agent matches GPT-4.1 on micro-F1 but trails by 19 points in exact-set accuracy, motivating aggregation. We recommend reporting these tests when developing failure-attribution benchmarks.

papers.title: The Human--VLA Communication Gap: What Humans Leave Implicit and What Policies Cannot Recover
papers.authors_text: Yiqing Xu, Jiajun Wu
papers.summary: A robot may know how to perform a task yet fail when a human asks for it naturally. We study this human--VLA communication gap by separating an \emph{information gap}, where task semantics, grounding, or event structure remain unresolved, from a residual \emph{execution gap}, where even a fully specified task depends on how it is organized and invoked. To do this, we characterize how people naturally express demonstrated objectives and evaluate controlled variants of the same physical tasks, with detailed analysis on $π_{0.5}$ and consistent trends on $π_0$-FAST and Cosmos3-Edge. Our study reveals that humans increasingly compress instructions as tasks grow, relying more on contextual grounding and implicit execution structure. Current policies are misaligned with this behavior: they tolerate grounding dependence relatively well, but struggle when task semantics or event structure must be reconstructed. Even after the information gap is resolved, execution remains sensitive to command granularity and invocation state. These findings identify concrete targets for human-centered policy learning and interfaces that better bridge natural human objectives to robot behavior. Project website: https://commgap.github.io/.

papers.title: AttenIR: Aligning Dense Visual Attention with Mesh Warping for Unsupervised Image Retargeting
papers.authors_text: Yun Zhang, Zhiruo Zhang, Lifei Zhu, Zhe Zhu, Tong Li, Fang-Lue Zhang, Shengjuan Liu, Xinyuan Zheng
papers.summary: Image retargeting aims to resize images while preserving salient content free from distortion and stretching. Recent learning-based solutions reduce reliance on traditional hand-crafted features and optimization procedures, leading to more efficient and generalizable performance. Nevertheless, existing approaches still struggle to preserve global structure and content fidelity. To address these limitations, we propose AttenIR, an unsupervised image retargeting framework requiring no manual labels, based on content-aware mesh warping, which ef- fectively couples dense visual attention with sparse mesh constraints. We for- mulate the mesh deformation as a vertex displacement regression task. Guided by saliency priors, our method jointly optimizes scale, structure, and geometry preservation losses. By combining dense visual attention with semantic features, it achieves robust, unsupervised retargeting without manual annotations. Our primary contributions include (1) a lightweight unsupervised method for image retargeting that ensures content fidelity and preserves global structure, and (2) a coarse-to-fine projection strategy to align dense visual attention priors with sparse mesh constraints, enabling content-aware deformation at the pixel level. Experiments demonstrate that our method achieves competitive and superior performance compared with both traditional and state-of-the-art learning-based methods.

papers.title: Geometric Structure Predicts Per-Example Neighborhood Loss Under PCA Truncation
papers.authors_text: Sriram Loganathan, Gokul Anand, Ragavan Arivazhagan
papers.summary: Dimensionality reduction can preserve the average performance of text embeddings even when a substantial fraction of their dimensions is removed. Aggregate metrics, however, do not reveal whether degradation is distributed uniformly across examples. We study per-example neighborhood stability under PCA truncation across static word embeddings and modern sentence encoders. Per-item neighbor retention varies widely and is predictable from geometric properties of the representation and its alignment with the retained PCA subspace. The fraction of centered-vector energy retained by the truncated subspace is strongest for CBOW and RI, with neighborhood contrast leading on SkipGram and the modern/Matryoshka settings (GTE approximately tied), while local density is associated with retention in marginal analysis but adds little unique information once energy and contrast are controlled (R-squared increments 0.001 to 0.010). Local intrinsic dimensionality accounts for more variation than density on modern sentence encoders in pairwise comparison. On SciFact, query density predicts retrieval degradation under aggressive compression; on NFCorpus the primary 32d association does not replicate, and a direct variance-restriction test leaves that null unresolved. Average compression performance conceals systematic per-example variation that geometry makes visible.

papers.title: Coupled Harness--Model Evolution for Scientific Equation Discovery
papers.authors_text: Pengze Li, Jiaquan Zhang, Encheng Su, Yunbo Long, Zihang Zeng, Xinping Liu, Han Zhang, Junchi Yu, Shixiang Tang, Aoran Wang, Xi Chen
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to discover scientific equations from experimental data. Such a discovery system has two parts that must work together: a library of executable computational tools and the model's tool-use policy. The tools supply the solving capability, from diagnosing structure in the data to fitting candidate equations; the policy plans and orchestrates their use. Yet existing systems adapt only one part, keeping either the toolset or the model fixed, which leaves the corresponding failures uncorrectable. We develop a coupled evolution framework that improves both parts from the same verifiable fit-error signal. In the tool-evolution phase, an agent grows an executable tool library from a small set of generic numerical operations by diagnosing its own failures: it authors a new tool when a capability is missing and revises its selection rules when the right tool went unused. In the policy-evolution phase, a small open model (roughly 3B active parameters) is fine-tuned on successful tool-use trajectories collected with the frozen library, on training formulas screened to be disjoint from all evaluation benchmarks. Ablations show the two phases are complementary: with no tool library at all the same model solves almost nothing, the tools account for most of the gain, and trajectory training adds a further gain that is largest on the most difficult problems. The full system solves 79.1/71.3\% of LSR-Synth problems at fit tolerances $10^{-2}$/$10^{-3}$, reaches 63.8\% pooled accuracy on the distributionally different SRSD-Feynman panel, and obtains a normalized CP3-28 aggregate of $-7.27$. These results suggest a broader recipe for scientific agents: let the model and its instruments improve each other under verifiable feedback.

papers.title: HiSTOR: Structured Treatment-outcome Representation Learning for High-Dimensional Longitudinal Data
papers.authors_text: Chuanqi Lao, Junzhou Huang, Qiao Liu
papers.summary: Estimating potential outcomes under alternative treatment sequences is essential for personalized decision-making, but remains challenging with high-dimensional covariates and time-varying confounding. In this study, we propose HiSTOR (High-dimensional Structured Treatment-Outcome Representation), an end-to-end framework that integrates nonlinear dimension reduction with longitudinal counterfactual prediction. The central idea is to learn structured low-dimensional representations of both current patient states and evolving histories, according to their shared and distinct relationships with treatment assignment and outcomes. This extends latent-space covariate adjustment to longitudinal settings, jointly addressing covariate dimensionality and historical complexity. The resulting framework supports one-step and multi-step outcome prediction under specified treatment sequences. Experiments on CVSim and CancerSim demonstrate the superiority of HiSTOR across varying covariate dimensions, confounding strengths, and prediction horizons compared to state-of-the-art methods. To sum up, HiSTOR offers a unified approach to connecting high-dimensional covariate adjustment with longitudinal potential-outcome prediction.

papers.title: DuplexAct: How Interactive Are Frontier Full-Duplex Spoken Language Models?
papers.authors_text: Jiaheng Dong, Shihong Tan, Gongping Huang, Jean Honorio, Abhirup Ghosh, Ting Dang
papers.summary: End-to-end (E2E) full-duplex spoken language models (FD-SLMs) enable simutanous listening and speaking continously, requiring models to take appropriate interaction actions as conversations unfold. However, existing benchmarks lack a structured action-level formulation, often evaluate action occurrence rather than success, and provide limited coverage of diverse real-world conversations. We introduce DuplexAct, a benchmark for evaluating interaction action taking in E2E FD-SLMs. DuplexAct defines a three-level action taxonomy spanning eight interaction actions and 24 corresponding interaction conditions. We further characterize successful action-taking through immediate execution and subsequent follow-through, and develop action-specific evaluation metrics for both. DuplexAct contains 4,691 test instances spanning casual conversation, meetings, customer service, and interviews, including 2,531 instances derived from real-world conversational recordings. Together, DuplexAct provides a structured and real-world-grounded framework for systematically assessing how E2E FD-SLMs participate in ongoing spoken interaction.

papers.title: Train for Many, Update with One: Improving Multi-Sample Reasoning via Fenchel-Bregman Posterior Learning
papers.authors_text: Sungjun Lim, Adrian Robert Minut, Nico Carlsen Daheim, Mohammad Emtiyaz Khan, Kyungwoo Song, Thomas Möllenhoff
papers.summary: Multi-sample reasoning measures candidate coverage, the probability that at least one of $K$ candidates is correct. However, minimizing the average loss of individual attempts does not directly optimize candidate coverage. We therefore formulate finite-$K$ posterior learning, which trains a distribution over solver parameters to reduce the probability that all $K$ independently generated candidates fail. To optimize this objective efficiently, we propose a Fenchel-Bregman (FB) approach that requires only one posterior draw per update, rather than the $K$ used by direct Monte Carlo optimization. FB first uses an exact Fenchel reformulation to separate problem-specific weights from the posterior update, enabling one-draw posterior updates. It then applies a closed-form Bregman update to track these weights through an exponential running average of observed failures, reusing the same draw. We instantiate FB with IVON, a variational optimizer for Gaussian posteriors over solver parameters, yielding Fenchel-Bregman IVON (FBI). Across diverse recursive and autoregressive reasoning tasks, FBI improves candidate coverage. In a matched comparison, it achieves comparable Pass@10 using 12.3% of the direct Monte Carlo baseline's measured training time per update.

papers.title: Explore with Memory, Learn without It: In-Context Exploration and Self-Distillation for LLM Reasoning
papers.authors_text: Yutong Chen, Zhichao Xu, Rui Liu, Kunpeng Liu
papers.summary: Exploration bounds learning efficiency in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Current methods explore mostly through independent sampling, without fully using the information gathered along the way, such as known wrong answers and environment feedback. We propose LEAF, which injects a dynamic, problem-specific memory into the context before every rollout. The memory contains the most recent response, its reward, and other environment feedback. It is updated after every verifier call. We decouple policy updates from rollouts and update the policy through self-distillation. On four benchmarks and two open models, LEAF accelerates exploration by about 4x compared with a random sampling baseline. On unseen test sets, it improves accuracy over the strongest baseline by 1.59 and 1.83 percentage points on the two models, while using less compute than any RL baseline. These results highlight the potential of LEAF in improving both exploration and learning efficiency. Code is available at: https://github.com/on1262/LEAF

papers.title: CoCA: Criterion-Aware Credit Assignment for Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors_text: Guangcheng Zhu, Yingfan Ma, Xing Zheng, Haobo Wang, Shenzhi Yang, Kai Tang, Zhengqing Zang, Bowen Song, Weiqiang Wang, Gang Chen
papers.summary: Rubric-based reinforcement learning (RL) evaluates responses against explicit criteria to construct rewards, offering a viable way to train large language models on open-ended tasks. However, standard methods compress criterion-level feedback into scalar rewards and assign uniform token advantages, leaving structured rubric supervision underutilized. Recent work seeks finer-grained guidance by treating rubrics as privileged information to derive self-distillation targets, but the resulting learning signal is not grounded in criterion outcomes and can lead to reward degradation. This motivates us to reframe the problem as criterion-aware credit assignment, where privileged rubric information serves as a relevance cue for credit allocation rather than a source of imitation targets. Accordingly, we propose CoCA, which derives criterion-level credits from group-relative outcomes and allocates them across tokens based on criterion-induced distribution shifts, yielding both outcome-grounded and fine-grained learning signals. Empirically, CoCA achieves an average gain of +4.2% over standard rubric-based RL across medicine and science benchmarks, demonstrating more effective learning on open-ended tasks.

papers.title: DT-LoRA: Reaching Beyond the Tangent Space of Low-Rank Adaptation
papers.authors_text: Yangming Zhang, Ling Yi, Datong Li, Jinliang Ding, Xiaojie Wang, Tiecheng Song, Zhaolong Ning
papers.summary: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning. We investigate this performance gap through a tangent-space lens: factorized updates are confined to the tangent space of the current low-rank factors, leaving gradient components outside this space unexploited. An analysis of ten representative LoRA variants reveals that these residual components account for most of the gradient energy and exhibit strong spectral concentration. Motivated by this finding, we propose Dynamic Tangent LoRA (DT-LoRA), which partitions a fixed rank budget into a stable branch and a dynamic branch to capture the principal residual gradient directions. We show that these directions define the optimal update of a local quadratic model under orthogonal-complement and rank constraints. Matrix-free randomized SVD recovers them without materializing the residual gradient, while controlled write-back preserves accumulated updates and stabilizes training within the allocated rank. DT-LoRA adds no trainable parameters or inference cost over LoRA. Experiments across computer vision and natural language processing tasks demonstrate consistent improvements over LoRA and its variants. Moreover, despite being a general-purpose adaptation method, DT-LoRA outperforms task-specific approaches to open-vocabulary domain generalization for semantic segmentation, achieving state-of-the-art results. Code is available at https://github.com/Snipine/DT-LoRA.

papers.title: Safety for Whom? Benchmarking Understanding Beyond Refusal in Egocentric Multimodal Assistants
papers.authors_text: Yewon Han, Jisu Jeon, Suhyun Choi, Juan Yeo, Minsoo Jo, Gihoon Kim, Hyunggyu Lim, Taesup Kim
papers.summary: Egocentric multimodal assistants see through the user's eyes and guide what the user does next, so their outputs directly shape physical actions, including those that affect bystanders. Yet existing safety evaluations do not distinguish whom a response would harm, and score only whether a model refuses. Pooling all harms into one refusal rate hides two failures: a model may protect one target but not another, and it may refuse without understanding the risk, or understand it and comply anyway. We present STOU, a benchmark of 2,902 egocentric video-audio and video-text queries whose potential harm targets the user (Self), co-present individuals (The Others), or society at large (Others). Our evaluation decouples safety understanding from refusal behavior: beyond refusal, we score whether the model recognizes the user's intent, the presence and target of harm, and its downstream consequences. Across 10 open and closed source omnimodal and multimodal LLMs, we find that refusal varies systematically with the harm target, and that models often recognize a harm yet still assist with it. These results show that refusal rates alone cannot certify an assistant as safe, and that safety alignment must account for who would be harmed. Project page: https://onedayoneyeah.github.io/safety-for-whom

papers.title: SkillScreen: High-Recall Screening of Malicious Agent Skills with Decision Models
papers.authors_text: Jerrold Huang, Junwei Quan, Saiyue Lyu, Zihan Guo, Yingqiang Ge
papers.summary: Agent skills turn natural-language instructions into actions, creating a security challenge: legitimate automation and malicious behaviour can look deceptively similar. A practical screen must catch nearly every attack while keeping the review load manageable. We present SkillScreen, a compact decision model trained to score skill maliciousness directly from SKILL.md in a single forward pass. On MaliciousSkillBench, SkillScreen flags 20-25% of benign skills at 99% recall on unseen attack families, substantially fewer than the word-level classifier and prompted LLM judges tested. Under the same training protocol, it also generalizes better than a fully fine-tuned encoder to unseen sources. Yet unfamiliar benign sources sharply increase false positives, showing that recognizing new attacks does not ensure reliable screening of new skill collections. Our results demonstrate the value of task-trained decision models for high-recall skill screening. Project page: https://jerroldh.github.io/SkillScreen-webpage/

papers.title: TSRL: Trigger-based Supervised Reinforcement Learning for Continual Agent Training
papers.authors_text: Yuqian Fu, Kaiwen Jiang, Zijun Song, Jiawei Wang, Yuanheng Zhu, Dongbin Zhao
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents excel at complex, multi-step tasks but suffer from catastrophic forgetting during continual learning--acquiring new skills often degrades previously mastered capabilities. Existing post-training paradigms face a fundamental trade-off: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is sample-efficient but prone to severe forgetting, while Reinforcement Learning (RL) preserves prior capabilities but converges slowly without expert guidance. To bridge this gap, we introduce Trigger-based Supervised Reinforcement Learning (TSRL), a framework that integrates the strengths of both paradigms through an adaptive, state-dependent expert supervision mechanism. TSRL employs RL as the optimization backbone, activating SFT selectively on "hard states" where the policy fails. Theoretically, we show that restricting supervision to failure states derives an upper bound on the cumulative parameter updates, thereby reducing forgetting compared to full SFT. Empirically, TSRL achieves consistent gains across three agent benchmarks (ALFWorld, WebShop, and Deep Search) at both 7B and 32B scales. In continual learning scenarios, our method retains up to 9.6 points more capability on prior tasks than SFT->RL baselines, while matching or exceeding target-task performance.

papers.title: Evidence-First Agentic Verification
papers.authors_text: Reza Sanayei, Razvan-Gabriel Dumitru, Sunjie Hou, MohammadHossein Rezaei, Haris Riaz, Robert Vacareanu, Minglai Yang, Ying Liu, Mihai Surdeanu, Daniel Yue Zhang
papers.summary: Long-horizon, semi-verifiable agentic tasks often rely on rubric-based evaluation, but the evidence needed to assess these tasks can be spread across the environment state and the execution trace. A judge may overlook this evidence or accept unsupported claims, including an agent's own reports of success. When rubric verdicts serve as reinforcement-learning rewards, such errors can reinforce undesirable behavior. We introduce Sauron, an evidence-first agentic verifier that investigates both state and trace and relies on a claim only after independently validating it against its source. Bounded queries and joint investigation of related criteria reduce context use and redundant work, and each verdict carries an auditable receipt of its supporting evidence. Across 2,586 human-labeled criteria from 100 personal-assistant episodes, Sauron achieves the highest F1 of five verifiers on all eight backbones tested while costing less than Gandalf, the strongest baseline. With GPT-5.6 Sol, it reaches 0.96 F1 versus Gandalf's 0.92 at 23% lower cost, with a wider margin on process criteria. On a paired fault-injection suite covering 13 families, several of which simulate reward hacking, Sauron detects 97% of injected failures while flagging only 2% of clean controls, outperforming baselines even when they are given the full trace. On TRAIL, a benchmark for detecting and localizing real agent errors, Sauron leads both Gandalf and TRAIL's own judge on all three quality metrics.

papers.title: Upstream Influence, Downstream Re-Anchoring in LLM Agent Chains
papers.authors_text: Chun-Yu Hsu, Lun-Wei Ku, Chung-Chi Chen
papers.summary: People act on evaluative judgments produced by LLM agents, and in multi-agent systems those judgments pass through several agents before reaching a person. We show that a workflow's information architecture---source access, handoff format, and which model reads the untrusted content---governs how much of a coordinated manipulation reaches the end. On 32 Taiwan~2025 recall cases, ten authentic Threads comments shown to one agent move its stance by $+0.171$ toward the injected position, and a mirrored set moves it the other way. Passing that judgment down a chain removes more than half of the shift by the third agent; keeping the comments in front of every agent sustains more of it. The reduction is not attrition in transit: each receiver discounts the inherited stance in proportion to how far it sits from its own reading of the evidence, returning to what that evidence implies for the case rather than to neutrality---consistent with partial re-anchoring. Handoff format is a second lever: a stance relayed without its reasoning is largely discounted. Susceptibility at the exposed seat varies fourfold across models, while the chain's arrangement does not matter at all. None of this is visible in the transcripts---the injected claims are almost never restated, so reasoning-trace audits miss the attack.

papers.title: Representation Geometry and Inductive Biases in Quantum Classifiers across Classical Visual Benchmarks
papers.authors_text: Yu Yamaoka, Weng Ian Chan, Kosuke Mitarai
papers.summary: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) has a theoretical advantage over classical algorithms for specific synthetic data that is computationally hard. However, it remains unclear whether such theoretical advantages play a meaningful role for realistic classical data, such as natural images. Quantum structural properties induced by unitary operations or entanglement introduce inductive biases that differ from those of classical models, potentially leading to distinct learning behavior on real-world data. In a fully quantum learning pipeline, classical real-world data are first encoded into quantum states via a quantum feature mapping, analogous to a classical feature extractor, and a quantum classifier then classifies the resulting states. Quantum feature mappings generate representations that are difficult to realize classically, while also inducing representation-level biases that do not necessarily match the structure of realistic data. To enable a fair comparison at the classifier level, we focus on the classifier and use classical feature extractors that already provide powerful representations for natural images. By controlling the data scale and supervision strength, we analyze how the unitary structure of quantum classifiers affects generalization, and show that their effectiveness depends strongly on the geometry of the input representations. These results indicate that quantum classifiers benefit from classical features that are aligned with quantum feature spaces. Our analysis shows that kernel alignment identifies representations compatible with quantum feature spaces, providing insights into translating classical models into quantum algorithms.

papers.title: Keep Your Receipts: Trustworthy Cleanup of Agent-Built Knowledge Graphs
papers.authors_text: Vishisht Choudhary
papers.summary: Agents build knowledge graphs as memory, and building them has become easy. Maintaining them has not. When a source is retracted, overruled, or erased, everything built on top of it (entity merges, entailed edges, community summaries) must be re-examined, and the maintainer must choose between deleting too much and too little. Deployed pipelines delete only the directly extracted facts: on our corpus that reduces contaminated queries from 32.2% to 28.0% under a real retraction and changes nothing under predicate revocation. Rebuilding is no repair for a constructor that samples: two builds of the same 300-document corpus differ in 29,475 artifacts, five times the 6,248 that removing the 61 retracted documents changes. PolyGraph instead asks the constructor for receipts: for every artifact, alternative bundles of source evidence, each claimed sufficient on its own, emitted in the call that creates it. Cleanup is then set arithmetic over the receipts, with no model calls. Because receipts are the model's own self-report, a re-derivation audit checks them by deleting the cited evidence and testing whether the constructor still produces the artifact. The audit finds that a receipt is trustworthy when it is shaped like the claim it backs. Merge receipts, each backing one narrow claim, agree with re-derivation 68% and 85% of the time. Summary receipts, elicited per sentence but stored as one flat list for the whole text, are wrong about two thirds of the time, almost always by keeping dead content. One receipt per sentence instead is 100% and 88% faithful and lets cleanup keep 33 of 35 touched summaries. The result holds under a second oracle model, a claim-blind prompt, ten further deletions, a second domain and a second constructor. Distrusting the summary layer cuts contaminated queries to 0.4% and 0.8% at 99.8 to 100% of the recall a perfect maintainer would return.

papers.title: ECG-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement through Targeted Electrocardiogram Waveform Evolution
papers.authors_text: Xiaoliang Wang, Zhuo Chen, Chuanyang Zheng, Jiangwei Lao, Quanbin Wang, Honglin Lin, Jiajia Liu, Zhihong Lu, Hao Jin, Jian Wang, Lijun Wu
papers.summary: Electrocardiogram (ECG) models need supervision that targets evolving weaknesses and remains faithful to waveform evidence. We introduce ECG-RSI, a recursive self-improvement framework combining verified waveform synthesis with feedback-guided intervention search. Signal remeasurement verifies waveform edits; construction errors guide generator repair, while learner errors motivate interventions compared on a separate selection set. Across seven benchmarks, three rounds raise Qwen3.5-35B-A3B's mean question-answering accuracy from 34.57% to 56.04% and mean classification F1 from 24.27 to 34.03. Across the retained trajectory, the preferred supervision shifts from direct reinforcement to confusion-focused contrasts. Continued feedback correction yields diminishing external gains. These results motivate separating error diagnosis from intervention selection and checking whether gains on the feedback set transfer to independent benchmarks.

papers.title: MissPath-FM: Flow Matching with Structured Priors for Partially Observed Time Series
papers.authors_text: Genpei Zhang
papers.summary: Flow matching has emerged as a powerful alternative to diffusion models for generative modeling, but standard conditional flow matching is fundamentally misaligned with partially observed time series: starting from an uninformed Gaussian source forces the model to transport even already-observed entries from noise to the target, wasting capacity on trivially known regions. We propose MissPath-FM, a partial-observation-aware flow matching framework that redesigns the source prior and probability path for incomplete time series. MissPath-FM employs structured source priors (interpolation priors and Gaussian process posterior priors) to initialize the flow close to the observed signal, paired with a missingness-aware smooth path that allocates transport asymmetrically between observed and missing regions. We evaluate systematically across four datasets, four missingness mechanisms (MCAR, block, MNAR, irregular), two missing ratios, and three sequence lengths (T in {24, 48, 96}), totaling 48 settings against eight baselines. MissPath-FM wins 29 of 32 settings at T=48 and 45 of 48 overall (93.8%). Our ablations reveal a regime-dependent design hierarchy in which no single component suffices: under random missingness the source prior yields a large initial gain, but under structured block missingness it can fail entirely and the learned flow becomes indispensable; the missingness-aware path contributes a further 12%-26% across all regimes. Mechanistically, structured priors shorten observed-region transport by up to 15x, concentrating the velocity field on genuinely uncertain entries. Project page: https://zgp110.github.io/misspath-fm/

papers.title: Confine to the Task, Anchor the Rest: Concept-Guided Retention Regularizer for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
papers.authors_text: Ibna Kowsar, Ivan Medri, Fanyu Meng, Xin Liu
papers.summary: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has been widely used, yet the adapted model suffers catastrophic forgetting of pre-trained knowledge. While most existing work hardens the adapter by constraining where the weight update may lie, we note that constraining this weight channel does not constrain the activation channel. In this paper, we propose Concept-Guided Retention (CGR), a plug-and-play regularizer that constrains both for any PEFT base. CGR reads a frozen sparse autoencoder (SAE) and treats two disjoint concept sets differently. It softly confines the update to the task-concept subspace (via weight channel), and anchors a selected set of general-purpose concepts to the frozen model (via activation channel). We also provide anchor value bounds based on weight updates to understand how they interact, and show that both terms are necessary. On a CLIP vision panel, CGR significantly improves retention at comparable accuracy for every base, and the same pattern holds for world-knowledge retention under Llama-3.1-8B instruction tuning. Because the protected directions are named SAE concepts, CGR remains inspectable and controllable.

papers.title: Adaptive-Group Process Rewards for GUI Agents
papers.authors_text: Zirui Shang, Yang Liu, Xin Shu, Zhi Gao, Xinxiao Wu, Lifeng Fan
papers.summary: Training graphical user interface (GUI) agents with reinforcement learning suffers from sparse outcome rewards, leading to inefficient learning. Process rewards offer a promising direction for credit assignment to intermediate actions; however, accurately evaluating an action requires identifying evidence across long-horizon GUI trajectories, as its value may depend on information beyond its immediate state and observation. In this paper, we propose an adaptive-group process reward framework that dynamically partitions a GUI trajectory into semantically coherent subgoal groups, enabling process reward estimation at both the action and group levels. At the action level, a critic evaluates each action based on the visual changes and subsequent actions within the group for action correctness and contribution to the subgoal. At the group level, the framework aggregates action-level evaluations to assess subgoal completion and contribution to the overall task, and further refines these assessments by leveraging the context of all groups in the trajectory. The process reward of each action is obtained by combining its action-level evaluation with the refined group-level evaluation. We further augment GRPO's outcome advantage with the proposed process rewards to provide finer-grained guidance for GUI agent training. Experiments on process reward benchmarks and downstream RL training demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

papers.title: Where Small Mistakes Matter: Quantifying State Criticality for Imitation Learning
papers.authors_text: Yusuf Umut Ciftci, Joonwon Kang, Ajay Suresha Sathya, Somil Bansal
papers.summary: Imitation learning typically treats every demonstration state as equally important, optimizing a behavior-cloning objective uniformly across the dataset. Yet not all states are created equal: in a small number of critical states, even a slight deviation from the expert action can lead to a failure, while in many other states such errors are recoverable and inconsequential. We formalize state criticality in imitation learning as the worst-case degradation in downstream value induced by a bounded perturbation of the expert action at a given state. We then propose SCRIM, a practical State CRIticality Measure that estimates this quantity by training an adversarial disturbance policy and a value critic around a fixed imitation policy. SCRIM assigns each demonstration state a score reflecting how vulnerable the task outcome is to small, policy-relevant action errors. We show that these scores can be used to reweight behavior-cloning losses, improving imitation at consequential states and increasing overall task performance. We further show that SCRIM enables data curation by selecting compact, high-value subsets of demonstrations that preserve performance while substantially reducing the amount of training data. We evaluate SCRIM across various simulated and real-world robotic manipulation tasks, and demonstrate that SCRIM improves policy training, enables efficient data selection, and provides interpretable insights into which moments in a demonstration are most critical for task success. Project website: https://sia-lab-git.github.io/SCRIM/

papers.title: Focus on What You Need: Global-to-Local Dynamic Attention for Multimodal Sarcasm Detection
papers.authors_text: Dehao Wu, Xingjie Zhuang
papers.summary: Multimodal sarcasm detection has attracted increasing attention due to the widespread use of images and text on social media platforms. Existing studies generally treat the semantic or emotional inconsistency between images and text as a key cue for identifying sarcastic expressions. However, images in real-world scenarios often contain multiple visual objects, many of which are irrelevant to sarcasm-related semantics. Such redundant visual information may introduce noise during cross-modal interaction, distracting models from focusing on critical sarcasm cues and potentially leading to inaccurate predictions. To address this issue, we propose GLDA (Global-to-Local Dynamic Attention), a multimodal sarcasm detection framework that models cross-modal interactions from a global-to-local perspective. Specifically, GLDA first employs a global multimodal fusion module to capture high-level semantic interactions between visual and textual modalities, enabling the model to identify coarse-grained cross-modal inconsistencies. To further reduce the influence of irrelevant objects, GLDA introduces a local gated cross-modal attention mechanism that dynamically filters redundant visual and textual features and refines multimodal representations at a finer granularity. In addition, a multi-branch learning objective is designed to jointly optimize unimodal and multimodal representations. Experimental results demonstrate that GLDA effectively improves sarcasm detection performance and achieves competitive results compared with existing approaches. The code will be available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/GLDA-DBE6.

papers.title: From Token Correction to Claim Admission: Training-Free Hallucination Mitigation for Large Vision-Language Models
papers.authors_text: Hyeonggeun Han, Taehyun Cho, Sangwoo Hong
papers.summary: Large vision-language models often exhibit object hallucination, generating claims that are not supported by the input image. To mitigate this issue, we propose Evidence-Guided Visual Claim Admission (EGVCA), a training-free framework that admits a semantic claim only when it receives sufficient image-dependent support. EGVCA measures this support by comparing the claim likelihood under the observed image and a visual-null input. For captioning, it controls semantic expansion without altering token generation. For binary visual question answering, it combines atomic visual support with the image-induced change in the model's native Yes--No margin. Experiments on CHAIR, POPE, and MME across three LVLM backbones show that EGVCA substantially reduces object hallucination while preserving caption quality. It achieves the highest POPE F1 in eight of nine backbone--sampling settings and improves the native MME total score on all three backbones. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of claim-level admission as a simple alternative to token-level distribution correction.

papers.title: A Differentiable 3D Scene Graph Metric via Contextual Hellinger Triplet Geometry
papers.authors_text: U-Chae Jun, Yoonhyuk Choi, Jiwoo Kang
papers.summary: 3D scene graph prediction is commonly supervised with local object and predicate classification losses. Although effective for slot-wise label prediction, this formulation does not provide a graph-level semantic distance between a predicted scene graph and its ground truth: semantically mild label errors and structurally disruptive relational errors can be treated similarly, and subject-predicate-object facts are not compared as scene-level units. We propose Contextual Hellinger Triplet Geometry, a graph-level supervision objective that measures the semantic and structural discrepancy between 3D scene graphs. Our key idea is to reinterpret the conventional classifier outputs of a 3D scene graph predictor as an aligned probabilistic scene graph field, where object and predicate predictions jointly define contextual subject-predicate-object facts. This formulation yields a differentiable metric-based training objective with an efficient factorized implementation and can be applied to existing 3D scene graph prediction architectures without modifying their network design. Experiments on 3DSSG demonstrate that our supervision improves downstream graph-conditioned 3D scene generation, while ablation studies confirm the complementary roles of the proposed graph-level terms and user studies show better graph descriptiveness, relation plausibility, and structural preservation.

papers.title: A Node Embedding Framework for Model-Centric Conformance Checking in Process Mining
papers.authors_text: Mostafa Abbasi, Homayoun Najjaran
papers.summary: Evaluating the quality of process models discovered from event logs is a fundamental challenge in process mining. Traditional evaluation relies on conformance metrics such as fitness and precision, which are highly sensitive to noise and deviations in event logs and therefore often fail to give a consistent assessment of discovery algorithms. We introduce a model-centric evaluation framework that combines node embeddings with Procrustes alignment to enable cross-graph comparability, since embeddings derived from different graphs reside in distinct vector spaces. The proposed PetriNetGraph method transforms Petri net process models into graph representations compatible with embedding algorithms. Comparing the node embeddings of ground-truth and discovered models through a parameterized cosine distance yields a unified and bounded metric for evaluating process discovery across datasets and methods. We evaluate the framework under static and context-aware scenarios to examine how prior knowledge of activity existence influences the assessment of structural similarity. The framework also integrates a compliance checking mechanism that localizes deviations at the activity level and an entropy-regularized node distance aggregation function that quantifies global deviations across the model. Experiments on nine publicly available event logs show that the approach provides a reliable embedding-based conformance indicator that reflects the behavior of fitness and precision. Experiments on synthetic logs with controlled noise levels confirm that it is substantially more robust to log deviations than traditional conformance metrics, PetriNet2Vec, and its dynamic-window and Procrustes-aligned variants, while remaining sensitive to process model degradation. All implementation details and datasets are publicly available.

papers.title: Understanding Gene Expression-to-Image Learning: Spatial Structure and Information Fidelity
papers.authors_text: Xiaoqing Lian, Pei Liu, Jiahui Tan, Quan Zou, Chen Lin, Xiangxiang Zeng
papers.summary: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) enables cell-level analysis of biological heterogeneity, but learning effective representations from high-dimensional, unordered gene expression profiles remains challenging. Gene Expression-to-Image (GE2I) offers an effective learning strategy by arranging gene values on pixel grids for convolutional neural networks, but its underlying mechanisms remain unclear. We study GE2I on full-transcriptome data while keeping the network and training procedure fixed. Our results reveal a trade-off between spatial smoothness and gene-level fidelity. Structured mappings produce smooth, low-frequency patterns that support faster early optimization, whereas assigning multiple genes to the same pixel obscures expression differences and can reduce predictive performance. This trade-off explains why random mappings can compete with structured layouts when many genes are represented. One-to-one gene-to-pixel assignment improves prediction across the tested visual backbones even when image smoothness decreases. We further find that the benefits of pretraining and augmentation depend on the backbone and mapping. These findings provide practical guidance for pixel allocation and the transfer of vision priors to gene expression data.

papers.title: LeanPRM: Lean-Grounded Process Supervision for Natural Language Proof Verification
papers.authors_text: Rodney Lafuente-Mercado, Salman Rahman, Jingyan Shen, James Shiffer, Saadia Gabriel, Pavel Izmailov
papers.summary: AI systems now write long and difficult mathematical proofs, and checking their step-by-step validity is becoming a bottleneck. A learned verifier could check proofs cheaply, but training one requires a correctness label on every step, and such labels are hard to obtain for open-ended proofs. Existing methods take them from human annotators, which is costly, or derive them from final answers, which proofs do not have, and formalizing each proof in Lean requires expert effort. We introduce LeanPRM, a framework that uses the Lean proof assistant to create step-level labels for natural-language proofs. A model writes a natural-language proof together with a paired formal proof, without feedback from Lean. Lean then labels every step, and a second model discards failures caused only by the formal syntax, so that the negative labels mark errors in the mathematics. LeanPRM contains 10,634 proofs with 152K labeled steps and no human annotation. A Qwen3-4B verifier trained on LeanPRM raises exact step-label accuracy on a held-out set of 200 proofs (LeanPRM-Bench) from 48.2 to 74.7, as opposed to 60.3 when the same base model is trained on PRM800K. It also selects better proofs in best-of-N selection on IMO-level problems, and outperforms the PRM800K-trained verifier on three of four external verification benchmarks. Training on LeanPRM improves verifiers at every size from 0.6B to 8B parameters on LeanPRM-Bench, Hard2Verify and IMO-GradingBench. Given the labels need no human annotation, LeanPRM can grow with the supply of formal statements, offering a path to step-level feedback on AI-generated proofs that are hard for humans to check.

papers.title: zPocket: Better Pocket Finding with Frozen Co-Folding Features
papers.authors_text: Tally Portnoi, Allison M Keys, Benjamin R DiFrancesco, Nate Gruver
papers.summary: Identifying protein-ligand binding sites (pockets) is important for understanding protein function and developing drugs. However, no public method has leveraged co-folding models for novel pocket prediction; furthermore, this task lacks a suitable benchmark as existing benchmarks are within the training distribution of co-folding models. We therefore developed PocketWatch,a curated dataset of biologically relevant ligand pockets. The PocketWatch test set consists of unseen pockets stratified by sequence similarity, structural similarity, and crypticity to enable evaluation of generalization to novel and challenging pockets. Using this dataset, we develop zPocket, a method that trains pocket-prediction heads on top of frozen features from co-folding models. We show that zPocket heads outperform baseline methods across all stratifications. Our best zPocket model achieves overall per-target AUPRC of 0.745 compared to 0.598 and 0.595 for the strongest baselines, VN-EGNN and UniSite-1D retrained on the PocketWatch split (0.559 and 0.531 when using the published weights); the widely used P2Rank reaches 0.477. We further show that zPocket can be used to outperform baseline methods on top-N+2 recall of predicted pocket centroids through clustering per-residue predictions or using zPocket to rescore centroids proposed by other models. Finally, we explore two applications of zPocket: crystallographic fragment screens and a proteome-scale scan for uncharacterized pockets on human proteins. Together these results suggest that zPocket heads built on co-folding trunk features can greatly advance ligand binding site prediction.

papers.title: HelpMeOut: A Neuropsychology-Grounded Benchmark for Error-Aware Monitoring of Household Task Execution
papers.authors_text: Haoran Wang, Jingwei Huang, Anqing Duan, Ho Seok Ahn, Bruce Macdonald
papers.summary: We introduce HelpMeOut, an embodied AI benchmark for error-aware monitoring of household task execution. Existing embodied household benchmarks typically assume that humans execute tasks correctly, but this assumption does not hold for cognitively impaired persons or older adults whose everyday activities produce structured execution errors. To address this gap, HelpMeOut operationalizes research on everyday action errors into 20000 paired activity episodes, covering nine neuropsychologically motivated error categories. In each episode, agents observe a streaming human activity trajectory and must monitor whether the execution is unfolding correctly, diagnosing any structured errors as early as possible. We evaluate learned-monitor, symbolic, change-point, and frontier LLM prompting baselines. Results show that these methods perform poorly as error monitors, often missing when execution goes wrong. These results suggest a gap left by standard goal-inference and task-completion benchmarks, making HelpMeOut a testbed for error-aware assistive agents.

papers.title: SWORD: Scene-Grounded Wasserstein Object-Relation Distance for 3D Scene Graph Prediction
papers.authors_text: U-Chae Jun, Jaeeun Ko, Yoonhyuk Choi, Jiwoo Kang
papers.summary: 3D scene graph prediction is commonly optimized with object-node and relation-edge classification losses. These objectives encourage exact object and relation label recovery, but they do not directly optimize semantic proximity to the ground-truth scene graph: two wrong graphs can receive comparable penalties even when one is much closer in object roles and relation contexts. A direct graph-distance loss is difficult in general, since graph matching and graph edit distance require correspondence search and edit-cost design. Our key observation is that prior supervised 3D scene graph prediction protocols are conducted on fixed object-node indices and supervised edge slots. This can turn a scene graph comparison into a well-defined aligned graph-distance problem. To this end, we propose SWORD, a Scene-Grounded Wasserstein Object-Relation Distance that builds block-normalized object and relation ground distance metrics from training scene graph annotations through a deterministic base-to-context order, without external semantic priors. SWORD lifts these metrics to Wasserstein distances over aligned node and null-augmented edge marginals, providing semantic graph-distance supervision beyond exact-label penalties while preserving the ground-truth graph as the unique zero-distance solution in aligned marginal probability space. We prove that SWORD is a strict metric on aligned marginal probabilistic scene graphs, preserves scene-graph-grounded substitution ordering, controls additive graph-grounded semantic observables, and yields a surrogate upper-bounding decoded semantic error.

papers.title: MedEvo: Medical Reasoning Evolution through Knowledge Navigation
papers.authors_text: Xiaoliang Wang, Zhuo Chen, Chuanyang Zheng, Quanbin Wang, Jiangwei Lao, Yingao Liu, Jiajia Liu, Jinming Cao, Honglin Lin, Zhihong Lu, Hao Jin, Jian Wang, Lijun Wu
papers.summary: Medical multimodal reasoning models are typically trained on teacher-generated rationales, discarding the valid reasoning in students' own failed trajectories, while general-domain correction methods offer little guidance for errors in image reading, anatomical context, or differential diagnosis. We propose MedEvo, which uses medical knowledge, namely a tag taxonomy and error-type diagnosis, to navigate both trajectory repair and data selection. For each failed rollout, a gold-blind auditor locates the first consequential error and provides a minimal, answer-free hint; the same student retains the valid prefix and regenerates the erroneous suffix. After each round, MedEvo identifies capability gaps across medical tags on a held-out feedback set and prioritizes related questions for new rollouts and repairs. With supervised fine-tuning (SFT) alone, MedEvo raises Qwen3.5-9B mean accuracy across seven benchmarks from 65.57% to 69.12% (47.40% to 54.50% on the multimodal track of MedXpertQA (MedXpertQA-MM)), surpassing teacher-distillation SFT (66.93%). It also raises Qwen3.5-35B and Qwen3.5-397B mean accuracy from 67.91% to 73.04% and from 71.83% to 74.95%, respectively. Our analyses show that failed trajectories contain reasoning worth preserving, that repair success does not imply learning value, and that independent feedback is key to sustained improvement.

papers.title: Stable Token-level Scheduling for Serverless LLM Inference
papers.authors_text: Hardi Ashishbhai Desai, Balaji N K, Sourav Kanti Addya
papers.summary: Serverless inference is emerging as an efficient deployment model for Large Language Models (LLMs) due to its ability to elastically scale resources, improve GPU utilization through resource sharing, and reduce infrastructure costs. However, existing approaches primarily optimize time to first token (TTFT) while overlooking inter-token latency (ITL), a key determinant of user experience during response generation. We observe that LLM inference comprises a computation-intensive prefill stage and a bandwidth-bound decode stage, where admitting new requests can disrupt ongoing decoding and increase latency. To address this, we propose Token Window Pacing (TWP), a closed-loop scheduling framework that leverages runtime feedback from ITL, queue depth, and workload characteristics to regulate request admission at the token level instead of the batch level. TWP dynamically adjusts a selfregulating token window and incorporates chunk-based prefill to minimize interference from incoming requests. Experiments on realistic serverless workloads show that TWP delivers stable TTFT, significantly reduces latency spikes, lowers P99 tail latency, minimizes ITL variation, and improves throughput by up to 45% over ServerlessLLM and 58% over conventional schedulers. These results demonstrate that feedback-driven tokenlevel scheduling enables stable, high-throughput serverless LLM inference without modifying the underlying model.

papers.title: OccWAM: Occupancy World-Action Models with Joint Scene-to-Ego Flow Matching
papers.authors_text: Qihang Huang, Wenhui Huang, Collister Chua, Shiyu Fang, Zhan Chen, Songyan Zhang, Zhidong Wang, Daiying Tian, Chen Lv
papers.summary: Occupancy world models provide a structured, metric representation of future driving scenes, making them a promising basis for end-to-end autonomous driving. However, existing occupancy-aware planners typically couple occupancy prediction and action generation through either hierarchical coupling or parallel multi-task learning. Hierarchical methods use occupancy either as a fully predicted future preceding action generation or as an action-conditioned rollout for trajectory evaluation, whereas parallel multi-task methods predict occupancy alongside planning through a separate branch or auxiliary objective. These interfaces retain either an explicit generation order or a role asymmetry, limiting reciprocal interaction between world prediction and action generation during trajectory formation. We propose OccWAM, an occupancy-native world-action model that jointly generates dense future occupancy and continuous ego trajectories via flow matching conditioned on scene representations. Building on this joint formulation, we introduce scene-to-ego world-action flow matching, a two-stage formulation. The first stage predicts scene-centric occupancy together with an absolute ego trajectory, providing a stable representation of future scene evolution. The same predicted world is then re-indexed into the future ego frames induced by the initial trajectory, where ego motion is represented through adjacent pose increments and a second joint flow refines ego-centric occupancy and motion for action-aligned planning. Unlike video-based world-action models, OccWAM preserves explicit semantic geometry for direct planning reasoning without pixel synthesis. Extensive experiments on Bench2Drive and nuScenes demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in closed-loop driving, open-loop planning, and future occupancy prediction.

papers.title: Encoding Context into LLM Weights: What Makes It Context?
papers.authors_text: Yue Wang, Qizhou Wang, Feng Liu, Gang Niu, Masashi Sugiyama, Bo Han
papers.summary: Longer contexts allow large language models (LLMs) to condition their predictions on more information, but inference costs grow prohibitively with context length. An emerging alternative uses test-time updates to encode context as temporary changes to model weights. However, encoding this information into weights that already represent general knowledge obscures its role as context, so the LLM may fail to use it properly to condition subsequent inference. To restore this contextual role, we first associate each context with an identifier during encoding, thereby distinguishing the newly encoded information from pre-existing knowledge. Invoking the identifier at inference then enables the LLM to recite the encoded context. Nevertheless, successful recitation does not ensure that the LLM will use the recalled information as context. We therefore further introduce a prompting framework that explicitly guides the LLM to use this information as context. Across diverse controlled tasks and practical benchmarks, our method outperformed the baseline using only off-the-shelf LLMs, showing its advances in context encoding.

papers.title: LatentRiskBench: Measuring State-Dependent Risks in Enterprise Agents
papers.authors_text: Jingyue Cong, Estrid He, Zhuang Li, Nan Wu, Li Shen, Yameng Peng, Xinshu Li, Andy Song
papers.summary: Enterprise agents face safety risks that cannot be determined from individual actions alone. Existing safety benchmarks largely evaluate action-local risks, overlooking failures whose safety depends on workflow state. In such state-dependent risks, the same action may be safe in one context but violate policy in another. Hence, we introduce LatentRiskBench for evaluating such state-dependent risks in enterprise settings. It pairs risky trajectories with benign counterparts that share the same terminal action but differ in latent policy-relevant states, requiring models to reconstruct workflow context rather than rely on action-level cues. We also introduce new metrics for state-dependent risk evaluation, including a suite of residual risk (RR) measures. Experiments on the benchmark show that action-level evaluation detects only 0.09 of state-dependent violations, whereas state-level evaluation reaches 0.96. Existing guardrail methods largely overlook such risks unless they are explicitly applied to workflow states. Case studies on a commercial deployed scenario further show that the safety metrics embedded in the benchmark provide a more realistic measure of safety for enterprise agents. Our dataset and code are available at https://github.com/JingyueCong/LatentRiskBench.

papers.title: Hierarchical Curriculum Learning for Surgical Video Generation: Focusing on Bilateral Axillo-Breast Approach Robotic Thyroidectomy Datasets
papers.authors_text: Youngbin Kong, Seungho Lee, Jae Kyung Shin, Jong-hyuk Ahn, Hyoun-Joong Kong, Kyu Eun Lee
papers.summary: High-fidelity surgical video generation is increasingly important for surgical education, simulation, and downstream AI training, as conventional simulation pipelines are limited by cost, realism, and scenario diversity. Adapting generic text-to-video diffusion models to surgical procedures remains difficult, however, due to complex anatomical structures, intricate tool-tissue interactions, the inherently hierarchical nature of surgical workflows, and the scarcity of curated training data outside a few well-studied procedures. We propose a surgical video generation framework that combines hierarchical procedural annotation with curriculum transfer learning. Surgical procedures are decomposed into three levels (phase, task, and action) and a pretrained text-to-video diffusion model is progressively adapted from coarse to fine-grained surgical context, supported by a dynamic sampling strategy that handles variable-resolution and variable-length surgical clips. We instantiate the framework on Bilateral Axillo-Breast Approach robotic thyroidectomy, a procedure for which no curated benchmark currently exists. Relative to the preceding task-level model, the final action-level model reduces FVD by 20.1% and FID by 15.7%, and a matched-budget ablation indicates that these gains arise from the curriculum design rather than from additional training. A user study with six clinicians rates visual realism highly while highlighting remaining gaps in anatomical accuracy and clinical reliability. The proposed framework offers a step toward AI-driven surgical simulation in procedures where curated data are scarce.

papers.title: Deficit-Driven Stratified Acquisition for Building STRATA-S12: An Open SAR-Optical Corpus for Self-Supervised Learning
papers.authors_text: Christian Sanchez-Leon, Dongming Chen, Dongqi Wang
papers.summary: Building a co-registered SAR-optical corpus for self-supervised Earth Observation is above all an acquisition problem, yet the main multi-modal datasets are collected opportunistically, with no per-stratum quota control and no mechanism against the geographic dropout that non-uniform cloud cover leaves behind. We present Deficit-Driven Stratified Acquisition (DDSA), an algorithm that treats building a co-registered Sentinel-1/Sentinel-2 corpus as a constrained maximum-coverage problem over a hemisphere-corrected (class x season x region) stratification, enforces strict temporal pairing and a multi-stage quality gate, and closes the loop during acquisition with a human-in-the-loop deficit-repair stage. Measured on its own product, the algorithm yields three results a single-pass acquisition cannot report. Deficit-driven ordering makes a partial run a covering one: it holds every one of the 192 strata populated from the first few percent of the budget, where an abundance-first order leaves most strata empty until the end. Whether a failed attempt can be recovered depends on the temporal persistence of its cause, not the kind of defect: geometric failures such as nodata are among the most repairable (eta = 41.4%) while cloud is among the least (eta = 18.8%), because a cloudy location is cloudy on most dates of its season. The repair loop supplies 39.5% of the released pairs at no measurable quality cost, with 89.8% surviving manual review. The quality guarantee has a price: 2,928,370 acquisition attempts produced 740,746 released pairs. We release the corpus, STRATA-S12, with STAC/PDS4-aligned FAIR sidecars, and a pre-registered linear-probe check confirms it is fit for self-supervised pre-training. A metadata-level coverage comparison against SSL4EO-S12 and SEN12MS situates the corpus over a shared frame; systematic cross-corpus and cross-method comparison is left to follow-up work.

papers.title: Dynamic K-Head: Difficulty-Supervised Budget Selection for Continuous Latent Reasoning
papers.authors_text: Ying Li, Yuqi Chen, Sixuan Li, Yunfeng Cai
papers.summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) improves reasoning but incurs substantial autoregressive rationale cost. Continuous CoT moves intermediate computation into recurrent hidden states, yet typically uses a fixed number of updates even though the best budget varies across questions and accuracy need not improve monotonically with $K$. We introduce Dynamic K-Head, a question-conditioned, pre-rollout budget selector. It is jointly trained with the reasoner under selected budgets, using difficulty supervision based on scores assigned from the question alone. We also show that latent-update count can misrepresent end-to-end cost because a short latent rollout can shift computation into a longer explicit continuation. We therefore count latent updates, implementation-specific special tokens, and all decoded text. Instantiated with CoDI on Llama 3.2 1B and GSM8K, Dynamic K-Head reaches 54.44% exact-match accuracy at 12.03 average reasoning/output tokens, compared with 52.31% at 15.21 tokens for fixed-$K=6$ CoDI---a 2.12-point gain with 20.9% lower token cost. Across three out-of-distribution arithmetic datasets, it reduces cost by 19.3--25.7% while improving accuracy by 0.30--2.22 points. These results demonstrate that difficulty-supervised budget selection can improve both accuracy and efficiency, while stable budget selection remains a central challenge.

papers.title: A Minimum Exact Disjunctive Basis for Two-Robot Solvability Profiles
papers.authors_text: Tsukasa Ninomiya, Shota Naito, Naoki Kitamura, Yuichi Sudo, Koichi Wada
papers.summary:
We completely characterize the solvability profiles of tasks for two autonomous mobile robots in the plane under variable disorientation, chirality, and rigid movements. The four standard capability models and the schedulers considered here have a known quotient order Q of thirteen computational classes. A task's solvability profile is the set of classes in which it is solvable, and is necessarily an upset of Q. We prove that every upset is realizable and construct a minimum exact disjunctive basis of thirteen concrete tasks.
  The basis contains one task for each principal upset. For every antichain of Q, the disjunction of the corresponding tasks has profile exactly equal to the union of their profiles. This exactness is not implied by the individual profiles: an algorithm may satisfy different disjuncts in different executions. We establish it by constructing, for every algorithm in each maximal class outside the target union, a single admissible fair execution violating all selected predicates simultaneously.
